Birth data

Every panel below reads from one chart. The Gochara and 12 Rāśiphal tabs work with no chart at all — a year of transits is a fact about the sky — so you can open those straight away.

Searches a built-in list of 34,000 cities held on this site — no external service. Sets the coordinates and the UTC offset that applied on your birth date, including historical daylight saving.

Sidereal · Lahiri ayanāṃśa · whole-sign houses

The city search sets the UTC offset that applied on the birth date, including historical daylight saving. If you type coordinates by hand, set the offset yourself.

Settings · ayanāṃśa and lunar nodes

Changes every sidereal position in the report. Lahiri is the default and everything on this site is validated against it; the others are offered so the choice is visible rather than hidden. An ayanāṃśa is a convention, not a measurement: the rate is astronomy, but where sidereal zero sits is a choice no observation can settle. The sixteen here span about 5° today — roughly 1.5 nakṣatra pādas — so they give different charts, not refinements of one. The Sūrya Siddhānta entries are several readings of one text, which describes the circle of asterisms as librating rather than precessing. Nirayana–Revatī is this site’s own, anchored on the dhruvaka of 359°50′ the Sūrya Siddhānta gives for Revatī, with the star moved by its real motion. The report’s Conventions section casts the chart under every one of them side by side, and the rule worth keeping is simple: if a reading flips when you change ayanāṃśa, it is an artefact of the convention rather than a conclusion.

Here & now asks the browser where this device is and casts a chart for that place at the present moment — useful for a praśna question, or simply to see the sky as it stands. The position comes from the browser, the clock and the UTC offset from the device, and the nearest town from the city list already on this page; nothing is sent anywhere. It needs the site to be open over https, so it will not work from a file opened directly off disk.

Fifteen of the animations are about the sky rather than about you: the eclipses, the tilt of the Moon’s path, the pañcā–aṅga, the phases. The nine that read your chart stay behind the form above, and each says why.

Cast a chart above, or open Vārṣika Gochara — that one needs no chart.



Vārṣika Gochara — a year of transits


This needs no birth chart. Gochara is where the nine grahas
actually are, so a year of it is a fact about the sky rather than about any
person. Pick a year and every rāśi ingress, every retrograde station and
every return to direct motion is computed from the same ephemeris that
casts the charts above — not copied from a table, so it follows whichever
ayanāṃśa you have selected.



  
  
  
  






Twelve Candra-rāśi readings


The same year read from each janma-rāśi in turn: which bhāva each graha
occupies counted from that rāśi, for how long, and which of the classical
gochara conditions are running. Every rule says which tier it comes from —
a BPHS verse, a note by the translator of this edition, or later tradition
— because transit doctrine is where those three are most often blurred
together.



  
  











Three layers, kept distinct. BPHS text = what the translated verses state · translator/commentary = notes in the Santhanam edition · study notes = plain-language synthesis or later analytical practice added here. Chapter citations refer to the uploaded Santhanam edition; verse numbers are OCR-affected, so confirm exact numbers in the PDF.
How the numbers are worked out: the chart engine, in detail — the ephemeris, the ayanāṃśa modes, the sunrise convention and what each divisional chart is computed from.
